job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up by eight because my little brother Kofi needs a lift to school, and then I'm at the desk in the box room of my parents' house in Birmingham. I finished a computer engineering degree in June with a pass. My final project was a drone that spots obstacles with a cheap camera, and it clips trees about one time in five. Most of my morning is applications and a chat with an AI model about whatever I'm building. In the afternoon I do paid work, fixing websites for small shops, which gets me about 200 pounds a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do the shop owners say about the work you do for them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad drives for a courier firm and my mum works at the hospital pharmacy. I've got two younger siblings, so the house is loud. I never did an internship, mostly because I took freelance jobs for friends, and I'm not sure employers count that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds right to me. I use AI tools every day, and they're good at the dull bits, but they aren't magic. I'd post a short note saying the hype is mostly marketing, then get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the plan holds. I keep applying, I keep freelancing, and the pass hurts less once I have proof of real customers. Birmingham has loads of engineering and software jobs. My parents help when I need it. I'd say I'm not stressed, but I'm not relaxed either, because I'm still earning less than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about 25 firms a month, including logistics and embedded systems, which suits my drone work. I'd turn my freelance jobs into a tidy portfolio and get two shop owners to write testimonials. I'd pay my mum a bit toward the house costs, and I'd put the rest into a savings account. And I'd use the AI tools even more for speeding up my routine work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. I've got a base of income and a base of confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not relaxed because you earn less than you should. What would 'enough' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 2,500 a month after tax, enough to rent a room with my mate Daniel and still pay my mum. At the moment it's about a third of that. I don't need a fancy car. I just want to stop being the person who asks for a lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you use AI for the dull bits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It saves me an hour a day, and I check the output. If I trust it blindly it breaks things, like the time it wrote a contact form that sent every message to the wrong address. I learned that from a shop owner shouting at me.

say: I'd say the hype is mostly **marketing** and post a short note.
I'd go back to work, with AI handling the dull bits.
think: The plan holds, and **real customers** matter more than the pass.
I'm not stressed, but I earn **less than I should**.
do: Apply to **25 firms a month**, including embedded systems that suit my drone work.
Gather **two testimonials** from shop owners and pay my mum a bit for the house.
feel: **Calm**, with a base of income and a base of confidence.
S0.quote: I don't need a fancy car. I just want to stop being the person who asks for a lift.
fieldNote: Daily AI user who **checks** output after a costly mistake.
Freelance work is his **proof** of skill, even without internships.
His goal is plain **independence**, not status.

steps.text: Send 25 applications a month, including embedded systems firms
Turn my freelance website jobs into a portfolio with two testimonials
Use AI tools to speed up routine web and test work
Save the surplus after paying my mum for the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already happening and people should learn the tools fast. In my group of friends I'd say the ones who use AI daily will get hired and the ones who don't will complain. I wouldn't say it online, because it sounds smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it hits the entry-level coding market hard. Firms hire fewer juniors, ask for AI skills as standard, and shift the dull work to software. But I'm a hardware-and-software person, so firms making devices, drones and sensors still need people who understand the real world. That's my lane, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise toward embedded and robotics, where software meets hardware. I'd finish the drone project properly and film it so it's a proper demo. I'd keep the freelance work but price it higher, and learn to use AI agents for the repetitive parts. And I'd apply to the three drone and robotics companies near Coventry first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I think I'm ahead of the average graduate, but ahead isn't the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ahead isn't the same as safe. What would make you feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A permanent job with a salary that covers rent, and a skill that isn't just prompting. If I had two years of real hardware experience I'd feel like it was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you price your freelance work differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop charging by the hour and charge by the job, since the AI makes me faster. If I charge by the hour I'd be punished for being good. A shop owner would pay 400 for a finished site, not 25 an hour.

say: I'd say people should **learn the tools fast**, and keep it among friends.
I'd skip posting online because it sounds smug.
think: Firms hire **fewer juniors** and ask for AI skills as standard.
Hardware-and-software firms still need people who understand the **real world**.
do: Specialise in **embedded and robotics** and film the drone demo.
Raise my **freelance prices** to a fee per job and apply to three robotics firms.
feel: **Uneasy**: I'm ahead of the average graduate, but ahead isn't safe.
S1.quote: If I charge by the hour I'd be punished for being good. A shop owner would pay 400 for a finished site, not 25 an hour.
fieldNote: Moves toward **hardware** because software juniors are exposed.

steps.text: Finish the drone obstacle project and film a proper demo
Charge freelance clients per finished site, not per hour
Use AI agents for repetitive website and testing tasks
Apply first to the three robotics companies near Coventry

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not sure anyone has the answer and that scares me. I'd say we need a plan for the first year, not in five years. At home I'd be calm in front of Kofi and my sister, because I don't want them frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it'd be heavy. If AI can do almost any thinking job by 2028, then my freelance work and the junior software jobs I'm aiming for are in the firing line. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so my drone and hardware skills would last longer, but only by a few years. I'm better placed than most, and I'd still be unsure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all-in on being the person who makes things work in the real world. I'd get a trade-adjacent certificate, like electrical installation or mechatronics, and offer installation and repair services to small businesses locally. I'd move all my spare money into a three-month cash reserve, and not spend a penny extra. I'd talk to Daniel about starting a small company together, so we're not a one-person bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel it in my chest on some mornings. But I'd also feel a weird energy, like it's finally time to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be calm in front of Kofi. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Kofi school still matters and we're not doomed, and I'd tell him to keep building. He's twelve and builds game worlds on his tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a company with Daniel actually sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smart installs for small shops: cameras, sensors, stock counters, simple automation. Not glamorous, but there's a lot of shops, and they won't use big firms. I'd use the AI to speed up quotes and docs.

say: I'd say we need a plan for the **first year**, not in five years.
At home I'd stay calm in front of my younger siblings.
think: My freelance work and junior software jobs are **in the firing line** in 2028.
Drone and hardware skills last longer, but only by **a few years**.
do: Get an **electrical installation** or mechatronics certificate and offer repairs to local firms.
Build a **three-month cash reserve** and plan a small company with Daniel.
feel: **Anxious** in my chest some mornings, with a strange energy to act.
S2.quote: I'd tell my brother Kofi school still matters and we're not doomed, and I'd tell him to keep building.
fieldNote: Moves from **software** to the physical world quickly, true to his adaptive profile.
Protects his **younger siblings** from the fear he feels.
Plans a small **company** to share the risk.

steps.text: Get an electrical installation or mechatronics certificate
Offer smart installs for cameras and sensors to local shops
Build a three-month cash reserve and stop extra spending
Use AI to speed up quotes, plans and paperwork for the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a strange gift: five years is enough time if you start now. I'd tell my mates the useful thing is to build skills that mix thinking and doing. I'd probably post a thread about what I'm learning, because teaching helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in a good spot. In five years I could have a proper job and some savings, and a small business on the side. When AGI arrives I'd have a track record, and robots for hands-on work would be about 2034, so there'd be still room for physical work. I'd feel more like a person who has choices than someone running scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get a hardware-and-software job at a firm that makes devices. I'd run the side business at weekends, install and repair work. I'd also study toward a chartered engineering route. I'd save at least 500 a month, and put some into a stocks-and-shares account. And I'd put my parents' loan on my list to clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. There'd still be worries, like rent, but the scary stuff would feel manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teaching helps you. What would you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The basics of using AI tools with real hardware. How to check the output, how to test, how to not blow up a sensor. People think prompts are the skill. The skill is knowing what 'right' looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the parents' loan be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They took a small loan for my laptop and the final year fees. About 4,000. They never say anything but I know every month it comes out. Clearing it is my first real goal.

I'd feel like someone with **choices** rather than someone running scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years sounds long but it'll go quickly. I'd say people should start experimenting now, not in year nine. I'd probably be the friend who keeps sending articles, which is annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel pretty good. A decade is a whole career stage: a first job, a second job, maybe a company. By 2036 I'd be 33, with some capital and experience. Robots would reach hands-on work around 2039. If I keep moving I'd always have something to pivot to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for three or four years, then try to start the installation company properly, with Daniel or another partner. I'd keep building small tools with AI, and I'd choose jobs that teach me different parts of a business. I'd save for a deposit, and I'd help Kofi and my sister with university costs, if they want to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd still be busy, but I'd feel like I was driving, not being driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your siblings with university. Would you tell them to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go if they want a particular thing, not just because everyone does. I'd tell them to pick something with people in it, like care or design. I'd be honest that I didn't get an internship and it hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not want to give up in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever technology does, I want Sunday dinner at my parents' place to stay the same. Mum does jollof and Dad falls asleep in front of the match.

I'd be the friend who keeps sending articles.

By 2036 I'd be 33 with some capital and **experience**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's the one where I can't prepare properly, and I've got a family counting on me to be fine. What would help is quick, cheap retraining and clear rules on how firms announce changes. Also a way to get work experience that isn't a gate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say the quiet bit. People think graduates who use AI every day are cheating. I'm not. I'm doing what a builder does with a power tool.

headlineQuote: People think graduates who use AI every day are cheating. I'm not. I'm doing what a builder does with a power tool.
portrait: Bilal is **23**, a computer engineering graduate with a pass, living in his parents' loud house in Birmingham with two younger siblings.
He uses AI **every day**, earns about 200 a week fixing shop websites, and checks everything after one costly mistake.
He is centrist and practical, and he **reprices** and re-specialises before the market forces him to.
Strong cushions and openings keep him **calm** in most pictures, except the 2028 one, where he feels it in his chest.
His plans keep returning to **hardware**, a small installation company and clearing his parents' loan.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most because he can't prepare and his family counts on him.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, cheap **retraining**, clear rules on announcing job changes, and work experience that isn't a gate.
